set.hook: The Roca brothers' three-star house in Taialà, forty years old this autumn and still all three on duty.
set.why: The restaurant opened in 1986 a few streets from the bar where the brothers' parents fed Taialà, and in 2026 it reached its fortieth year. Joan Roca marked it on 5 October at San Sebastián Gastronomika with a menu of forty small dishes, served with augmented reality at the table. Josep runs the cellar, Jordi the sweets, and the house twice topped the World's 50 Best list, in 2013 and 2015.
set.verdict: For the one guest dinner a trip is planned around. Take the Festival menu with Josep's pairing, and ask on booking whether the forty-dish anniversary menu is running on your date.

set.hook: A forty-year-old family house on Bonastruc de Porta, starred since 2007, son now at the stoves.
set.why: Pere Massana and Ana Roger opened on Carrer Bonastruc de Porta in September 1986, and the duck breast that is still on the card dates from that first year. set.hook: El Celler's back catalogue served in an 1893 hilltop fort ten kilometres north of Girona.
set.why: The Rocas took over the military fortress on the hill of Sant Julià de Ramis and opened Esperit Roca in 2024, with a hotel, a cellar under the dome, a distillery and a second restaurant, Fontané, named for their mother. Head chef Raül Sillero calls it El Celler's library of dishes: two menus, one six savoury and two sweet, the other the reverse, rotating with the seasons. Opinionated About Dining ranked it eighth among Europe's new restaurants for 2026.
set.verdict: For guests who cannot get into El Celler but want its classics. Go at lunch for the view and take the savoury menu for Toda la gamba.

set.hook: The Roca brothers' plain-spoken Catalan bistro on Plaça de l'Oli, cooking their mother's dishes.

set.hook: The Roca parents' 1967 neighbourhood bar in Taialà, still serving a weekday menú.
set.why: Josep Roca and Montserrat Fontané opened this bar on the Taialà road in 1967, and their three sons grew up behind its counter, doing homework among the pans. It remains a casa de menjars: a fixed weekday lunch of two courses and dessert that changes daily, eaten by locals and by El Celler's own brigade, stagiers included, who walk over between services. Montserrat, born 8 June 1936, turned ninety this year.
set.verdict: For crew who want the Roca story at bar prices. Go for the weekday menú, ideally on fish day, and do not expect the brothers.

set.hook: A family table opened in 1920 beside the Mercat del Lleó, cooking the market's morning haul.
set.why: Can Marquès opened in 1920, before the Mercat del Lleó it now faces was built, and the fourth generation of the same family runs it. The menu follows what the market across the square sells that morning: salt-and-pepper botifarra under melted brie, duck breast with port, salt cod with samfaina. Thursday is rice day, and a cheap weekday set lunch with bread, drink and coffee is what fills the room.
set.verdict: For crew shopping the Lleó who want a working lunch nearby. Go on a Thursday for the rice; expect slow service when it is full.

set.hook: Girona's oldest family restaurant, on the arcaded Plaça de la Independència since 1892.
set.why: The same family has cooked on Plaça de la Independència since 1892, five generations on, and the house is on Catalonia's register of centenary restaurants. The card has barely moved: duck with pears, roast lamb shoulder, cuttlefish with peas, salt cod under garlic mousseline, and the xuixo, Girona's cream-filled fried pastry. The grandmother's canelons are sold under the house name to take away.
set.verdict: For a relaxed lunch on the square with guests who want the classics. Order duck with pears and finish with the xuixo; book a terrace table.

set.hook: The Els Tinars family's town fonda under the Voltes d'en Rosés: porrons, cured meats, weekly rice.
set.why: In April 2025 the Gascons family, who run starred Els Tinars and Bell-lloc out on the road to the coast, opened their first restaurant inside a town: an old inn under the Voltes d'en Rosés. Marc Gascons cooks plain Catalan food here. Tomatoes hang ready for rubbing on bread, porrons go round, and cured meats from Toni Seli in Torroella de Montgrí come to the table for diners to help themselves. The rice changes every week with the market.
set.verdict: For a group dinner that wants Catalan basics done properly. Share the charcuterie and the rice a la llauna, and drink from the porró.

set.hook: Two El Celler veterans' seasonal Catalan bistro on Carrer dels Calderers, by Sant Feliu.
set.why: Adrià Edo and Júlia Trota spent more than six years at El Celler de Can Roca, he in the kitchen and she in the dining room, until the pandemic; then they opened this room of about thirty-five seats on Carrer dels Calderers. set.hook: The former Nu on Abeuradors, now Nexe: contemporary carte built on small local producers.
set.why: This was Pere Massana's second room, Nu, until 2022, when his kitchen team took it over and renamed it Nexe, Catalan for link. summit.title: Three stars, two singles
summit.story: Girona's starred cooking runs from a three-star house in a suburb to two single stars in town. El Celler de Can Roca opened in 1986 near the Roca parents' bar in Taialà, holds three MICHELIN stars and marked forty years on 5 October 2026 with a menu of forty small dishes. Massana opened on Carrer Bonastruc de Porta the same year, has held a star since 2007 and this spring passed the stoves from Pere Massana to his son Pere. Divinum started as a wine bar on Carrer Argenteria in 2001 and won its star in the 2025 guide in a vault under the old Casino. The 2027 list is announced on 24 November 2026.
summit.where: El Celler de Can Roca, Girona; Massana, Girona; Divinum, Girona

roca.title: Three rungs of Roca
roca.story: The Roca family now feeds Girona at three price points. Can Roca, the bar Josep Roca and Montserrat Fontané opened in Taialà in 1967, still serves a cheap weekday menú, and El Celler's own brigade eats lunch there. Normal, opened in 2021 on Plaça de l'Oli, has Elisabet Nolla cooking the dishes of the Roca grandmother and mother and holds a Repsol Sol. Up the hill at Sant Julià de Ramis, Esperit Roca serves El Celler's back catalogue inside an 1893 fort: one MICHELIN star since the 2025 guide, two menus that turn with the seasons, and eighth place among Europe's new restaurants on the 2026 Opinionated About Dining list.
roca.where: Can Roca, Girona; Normal, Girona; Esperit Roca, Sant Julià de Ramis

houses.title: Family houses, market cooking
houses.story: Girona's long-running tables cook from the market and keep the same dishes for decades. Casa Marieta has served duck with pears on Plaça de la Independència since 1892, run by the fifth generation of one family. Can Marquès opened in 1920 beside the site of the Mercat del Lleó and still sets Thursday aside for a rice made from what the stalls sold. The newest, Fonda Cal Ros, opened in April 2025 under the Voltes d'en Rosés, where the Gascons family of starred Els Tinars pass porrons round, hang tomatoes for bread and serve Torroella de Montgrí cured meats for diners to help themselves.
houses.where: Casa Marieta, Girona; Can Marquès, Girona; Fonda Cal Ros, Girona

chefs.title: Rooms the cooks choose
chefs.story: Girona's cooks eat in small rooms run by people they trained with. Dit i Fet, on Carrer dels Calderers, belongs to Adrià Edo and Júlia Trota, who spent more than six years at El Celler before opening; Joan Roca names it as where he eats in town. SAFO, by Plaça del Vi, pairs Marietta Richter's Mexican and Catalan share plates with Víctor Martín's natural wines, and won the emerging-chef Cuiner award in 2024. Nexe, on Carrer d'Abeuradors, is Pere Massana's former Nu, taken over by his kitchen team in 2022 and renamed for the link between diners and small local producers; its 2026 status still needs a phone call.
chefs.where: Dit i Fet, Girona; SAFO, Girona; Nexe, Girona
